title: Teach For Uganda STEM Fellowship 2026: Fully Funded STEM Teaching Opportunity for Young Women in Uganda.
summary: The Teach For Uganda STEM Fellowship 2026 is an opportunity for young women with backgrounds in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) to develop their teaching, leadership and professional skills while contributing to improved secondary education in Uganda. Implemented by Teach For Uganda under the Leaders in Teaching Program , the STEM Fellowship is designed to address the need for more capable, committed and well-supported STEM teachers in Uganda, with a particular emphasis on increasing the participation and leadership of women in STEM education. The pilot programme is supported by the Mastercard Foundation and implemented through a consortium led by the Luigi Giussani Foundation and other education partners. The fellowship combines classroom teaching, professional development, coaching and leadership development. Fellows are placed in secondary schools and supported to become effective teachers, mentors and role models for learners, particularly girls who may face barriers to participating confidently in STEM subjects. What Is the Teach For Uganda STEM Fellowship? The Teach For Uganda STEM Fellowship is a pilot programme focused on strengthening STEM teaching in Uganda s secondary schools. The programme recognises that Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics are increasingly important to education, employment, innovation and national development. However, access to quality STEM education remains uneven, particularly for learners in underserved communities. The fellowship therefore seeks to recruit young people with strong STEM backgrounds and develop them into teachers and education leaders. Participants are not simply placed in classrooms and expected to teach independently. The fellowship provides structured preparation, coaching and continuous professional development to help Fellows build the skills required to become effective educators. The programme also creates a pathway for young women with STEM backgrounds to enter education, take on leadership responsibilities and become visible role models for girls interested in science and technology. Why STEM Education Matters in Uganda STEM subjects play an increasingly important role in preparing young people for a changing world. Science, technology, engineering and mathematics influence how people: Understand the world around them Solve complex problems Develop new technologies Create businesses and employment opportunities Respond to social and environmental challenges Participate in the future workforce Develop innovative solutions Contribute to national development Despite the importance of STEM education, many learners continue to encounter barriers that affect their participation and confidence. Girls in underserved communities can face additional challenges, including limited access to role models and learning environments that encourage them to pursue STEM-related opportunities. The Teach For Uganda STEM Fellowship seeks to address some of these challenges by bringing more talented STEM graduates and young professionals into secondary-school classrooms. Through effective teaching and mentorship, Fellows can help learners understand that STEM is not simply about memorising formulas or concepts. Instead, STEM can be practical, creative and connected to real-world challenges. A Focus on Girls and Women in STEM One of the distinctive aspects of the STEM Fellowship is its emphasis on increasing the participation and visibility of young women in STEM education. The programme recognises that representation matters. When girls encounter women who are teaching science, mathematics and other STEM-related subjects, they can see examples of women actively participating in fields that have historically had gender-related participation gaps. The fellowship therefore seeks to create opportunities for young women to: Teach STEM subjects Become classroom leaders Mentor learners Encourage girls to participate in STEM Serve as positive role models Develop their own leadership abilities Contribute to education reform and community change The broader goal is to strengthen both the teacher pipeline and the participation of girls in STEM learning. About the STEM Fellowship Pilot The STEM Fellowship operates as an intentional pilot under the Leaders in Teaching Program . As a pilot, the programme provides Teach For Uganda with an opportunity to test the effectiveness of a leadership-focused fellowship model within secondary STEM education. The organisation can use lessons and evidence generated through the programme to understand: How STEM teachers can be effectively recruited How new teachers can be prepared for classroom responsibilities What types of coaching and professional development are useful How leadership development can strengthen teaching How STEM learning can become more learner-centred How girls participation in STEM can be encouraged How the fellowship model could potentially be strengthened and expanded The pilot is therefore not only intended to benefit individual Fellows. It is also designed to generate learning that can contribute to longer-term improvements in Uganda s education system. What Fellows Will Do STEM Fellows will be placed in secondary schools where they will contribute directly to teaching and learner development. Their responsibilities and experience are expected to involve more than delivering lessons. Fellows will be supported to develop classrooms where learners can: Ask questions Explore ideas Test concepts Solve problems Connect classroom learning with real-life situations Develop confidence Become more curious about STEM Participate actively in the learning process The programme encourages Fellows to use learner-centred and inquiry-based approaches rather than relying exclusively on memorisation. Training, Coaching and Professional Development A key component of the fellowship is professional preparation and ongoing support. Fellows receive structured training, coaching and continuous professional development to help them grow into effective educators. This support is intended to help Fellows strengthen both their technical knowledge and their teaching abilities. Areas of development include: Classroom leadership STEM teaching Learner-centred education Inquiry-based learning Professional growth Leadership Mentorship Community engagement Problem-solving Education equity This combination makes the fellowship a leadership-development pathway as well as a teaching programme. One-Year Postgraduate Diploma in Education Successful Fellows must be willing to undertake a one-year, fully funded Postgraduate Diploma in Education (PGDE) during their first year of enrolment. This is an important part of the professional development pathway. The PGDE can provide Fellows with formal training in education and pedagogy while they develop their practical experience as teachers. Because the programme specifies that the PGDE is fully funded, Fellows who meet the programme requirements do not have to pay for this training themselves. The Teach For Uganda Approach Teach For Uganda views teaching as a form of leadership. Under the STEM Fellowship, this philosophy means that teachers are expected to combine strong subject knowledge with: Classroom leadership Creativity Commitment to learner development Community engagement Problem-solving Continuous learning Advocacy for education equity The programme aims to develop teachers who can influence not only what happens during individual lessons but also how learners perceive themselves and their future opportunities. Learner-Centred STEM Teaching The fellowship promotes learner-centred approaches to STEM education. Instead of positioning learners as passive recipients of information, Fellows are encouraged to create classrooms where students actively participate in the learning process. This can include encouraging students to: Ask questions about concepts they encounter. Investigate problems. Test ideas. Explore possible solutions. Connect academic concepts with everyday experiences. Work through challenges. Develop confidence in their ability to solve problems. Such an approach can help make STEM learning more practical and engaging. Community-Based Leadership The fellowship also encourages Fellows to contribute to community-rooted solutions that can improve learning. This reflects the programme s broader leadership philosophy. Rather than viewing education challenges only from inside the classroom, Fellows are encouraged to understand the communities they serve and consider how local circumstances influence educational outcomes. This can help Fellows develop leadership skills that extend beyond traditional teaching responsibilities. What Makes the STEM Fellowship Different? The programme identifies several areas that distinguish the STEM Fellowship. 1. STEM Subject Focus The fellowship is specifically designed to strengthen teaching in science and mathematics-related areas and develop a stronger pipeline of STEM educators. 2. Girls Leadership The programme places particular emphasis on creating pathways for young women to enter STEM teaching and become leaders and role models. 3. Classroom Impact Fellows are prepared to improve how STEM subjects are taught and experienced by learners. 4. Leadership Development The fellowship aims to develop leaders who can contribute to education change beyond their immediate classroom responsibilities. 5. Systems Learning Because the programme is a pilot, Teach For Uganda intends to learn from the experience and use evidence from the initiative to inform future development and potential expansion of the model. Who Is Teach For Uganda Looking For? The programme is looking for young leaders who believe education can contribute to Uganda s future. Ideal candidates should demonstrate a combination of STEM knowledge, leadership potential and commitment to education equity. Teach For Uganda highlights candidates who are: Passionate about education equity Strong in STEM knowledge Willing to develop their teaching abilities Committed to supporting learners Particularly interested in supporting girls in STEM Open to coaching and constructive feedback Committed to continuous learning Willing to teach in secondary schools Flexible about school placement Interested in contributing to broader education change Ready to serve underserved communities The programme is particularly committed to developing pathways for young women with STEM backgrounds. VISIT HERE, for more imformation. Eligibility Requirements for the Teach For Uganda STEM Fellowship Applicants must meet the mandatory eligibility requirements set by the programme. 1. Ugandan Citizenship or Refugee Status Applicants must be either: A female Ugandan citizen , or A refugee currently residing in Uganda . This means the programme is not presented as an open international fellowship for applicants from other countries. 2. Bachelor s Degree in a STEM Field Applicants must hold a Bachelor s degree in a STEM field . The degree must have been completed with a minimum CGPA of 3.0 . Applicants should therefore have an academic background that is relevant to Science, Technology, Engineering or Mathematics. 3. Age Requirement Applicants must be between 22 and 27 years old at the time of application . Candidates outside this age range would not meet the stated mandatory age criterion. 4. English Language Proficiency Applicants must be proficient in English . English proficiency is important because Fellows will teach in secondary-school classrooms and participate in training and professional development. 5. Flexibility on School Placement Applicants must be willing to be placed in any USE (Universal Secondary Education) secondary school . This means candidates should be prepared to serve in the school location assigned to them rather than requiring placement in a particular school or area. Flexibility regarding placement is therefore an important part of the fellowship. 6. Commitment to Education Equity and Leadership Applicants should demonstrate a genuine interest in: Education equity Leadership Community change Supporting learners STEM education Girls participation in STEM The programme is intended for candidates who want to contribute to educational improvement rather than simply obtain teaching experience. 7. Willingness to Undertake the PGDE Applicants must be willing to undertake the one-year, fully funded Postgraduate Diploma in Education during their first year of enrolment. This is a mandatory component of the programme. Benefits of the Teach For Uganda STEM Fellowship The fellowship provides several professional and educational benefits to successful participants. Fully Funded Postgraduate Education Fellows are supported to undertake a one-year Postgraduate Diploma in Education during their first year. The PGDE is described as fully funded under the fellowship. Teaching Experience Participants gain practical experience teaching in secondary schools. This can help STEM graduates develop real-world classroom experience and understand the responsibilities involved in education. Professional Development Fellows receive training, coaching and continuous professional development. This gives participants opportunities to strengthen their teaching and leadership skills over time. Leadership Development The fellowship is structured as a leadership pathway. Participants are expected to develop skills that can help them contribute to education and community change beyond their classroom roles. Mentorship and Coaching Ongoing coaching and support provide Fellows with guidance as they transition into teaching and develop professionally. Opportunity to Inspire Girls Women participating in the fellowship have the opportunity to become visible STEM role models for girls in secondary schools. This can contribute to broader efforts to encourage girls to develop confidence and interest in science and technology. Contribution to Education Equity Fellows serve in secondary-school settings, including underserved communities, allowing them to contribute directly to efforts aimed at improving educational opportunities. Participation in a Broader Education Movement The STEM Fellowship forms part of Teach For Uganda s wider work to advance equitable access to quality education. Fellows therefore become part of a broader movement focused on education leadership and systemic change. Leaders in Teaching Program The STEM Fellowship is implemented under the Leaders in Teaching Program , a flagship initiative supported by the Mastercard Foundation . The programme is implemented through a consortium led by the Luigi Giussani Foundation . The Leaders in Teaching Program brings together education partners working to strengthen secondary education through areas such as: Teacher recruitment Teacher training Leadership development Teacher motivation Professional support System-level education support Teach For Uganda s contribution focuses on strengthening the teacher pipeline by recruiting, preparing and mentoring STEM teachers who demonstrate both subject mastery and leadership potential. Teach For Uganda s Role Teach For Uganda brings more than a decade of experience in leadership development and classroom placement to the STEM Fellowship pilot. Through this initiative, the organisation is applying its experience to the specific challenge of strengthening secondary STEM education. The programme therefore represents an expansion of Teach For Uganda s work into secondary education and a deeper focus on STEM teaching and girls education. Vision for the STEM Fellowship Pilot Teach For Uganda describes the STEM Fellowship as the beginning of an important shift in its work. The initiative expands the organisation s focus into: Secondary education STEM education Girls education Women s leadership Teacher development Education systems strengthening The organisation aims to learn from the pilot, strengthen the model and potentially develop pathways that can support more learners, schools and communities over time. The broader vision is based on the idea that improving education depends not only on getting children into school but also on the quality of learning, the people leading that learning and the opportunities learners can envision for themselves. Is the STEM Fellowship Free? Yes. Teach For Uganda states that all services provided under the STEM Fellowship are free of charge . There are no fees associated with: Registration Training Scholarships Other services provided through the programme Applicants should therefore be cautious of anyone claiming to represent the programme and requesting payment for registration or participation. For questions or concerns about the STEM Fellowship, Teach For Uganda provides the recruitment contact: Email: recruitment@teachforuganda.org How to Apply for the Teach For Uganda STEM Fellowship Interested and eligible applicants should submit their applications through the official application portal provided by Teach For Uganda. The application link provided by the programme is: APPLY HERE. Applicants should ensure that they meet all mandatory eligibility requirements before submitting an application. In particular, prospective candidates should verify their: Ugandan citizenship or refugee status in Uganda Female eligibility requirement STEM Bachelor s degree Minimum CGPA of 3.0 Age between 22 and 27 English proficiency Willingness to accept placement in any USE secondary school Commitment to education equity and leadership Willingness to undertake the fully funded one-year PGDE Important Application Information The fellowship is specifically designed around the needs of Uganda s secondary education system. Applicants should therefore understand that this is not simply a general graduate scholarship or academic fellowship. Successful participants will be expected to engage with teaching, classroom leadership, professional development and community service. The requirement to be flexible about school placement is particularly important for applicants who may be considering the programme from outside the location where they currently live. Conclusion The Teach For Uganda STEM Fellowship 2026 provides a structured pathway for young women with STEM backgrounds to enter secondary education, develop teaching and leadership skills, and contribute to improving STEM learning in Uganda. The fellowship combines classroom placement with training, coaching, professional development and a fully funded one-year Postgraduate Diploma in Education. It also places a strong emphasis on girls participation in STEM by creating opportunities for women to become teachers, mentors and role models. As a pilot under the Leaders in Teaching Program, the initiative also has a broader systems-level purpose. Teach For Uganda aims to learn from the fellowship and use evidence from the programme to strengthen the teacher pipeline and inform future approaches to secondary STEM education. For eligible candidates who are passionate about education equity, STEM, leadership and community change, the fellowship provides an opportunity to develop professionally while contributing directly to Uganda s education sector. Prospective applicants should carefully review the eligibility requirements and submit their application through the official application portal when applications are open. The programme states that participation and all associated services are free of charge. For more OFY Fellowship opportunities, CLICK HERE. title: Harvard Loeb Fellowship 2027–28: Fully Detailed Guide to Eligibility, Application Process, Deadline and What Applicants Need to Know
summary: The Harvard Loeb Fellowship 2027–28 is now accepting applications from experienced professionals whose work is focused on improving the built and natural environment and creating meaningful social impact. Hosted through the Harvard Graduate School of Design (GSD), the Fellowship is designed for mid-career practitioners who want to step back from their regular professional responsibilities, reflect on their experience, develop new skills, explore ideas, and prepare for the next stage of their careers. For the 2027–28 Fellowship year, applications are open until Tuesday, January 5, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time (ET) . There is no application fee , and international candidates are encouraged to apply. The Loeb Fellowship is particularly distinctive because it is not structured as a conventional academic fellowship, artist residency, or sabbatical program. Instead, it is designed for established practitioners who are already active in their professions and who have demonstrated the ability to contribute to their fields and communities. What Is the Harvard Loeb Fellowship? The Loeb Fellowship is a mid-career professional development opportunity associated with Harvard University s Graduate School of Design. It brings experienced practitioners into an environment where they can reassess what they have learned, expand their capabilities, engage with new ideas, and plan the next stage of their professional work. The program is aimed at individuals whose professional activities involve designing, planning, preserving, developing, critiquing, or otherwise influencing the places and environments in which people live, work, and interact. The Fellowship recognizes that improving the built and natural environment requires contributions from many different professional disciplines. Consequently, applicants do not have to be architects or designers to be considered. The program specifically identifies professionals such as: Urban designers Public artists Developers Journalists Civic leaders Architects Landscape architects Urban planners Policymakers Community development leaders The Fellowship also has a broad understanding of professional practice and social impact. Previous or potential applicants may come from less traditional backgrounds, including fields such as theatre, documentary filmmaking, journalism, and public art. Harvard Loeb Fellowship 2027–28 Deadline The application deadline for the 2027–28 Harvard Loeb Fellowship is January 5, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. ET . Applicants should pay close attention to the deadline because the recommendation letters have a separate deadline. Key deadlines include: Main application deadline: Tuesday, January 5, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. ET Recommendation deadline: Tuesday, January 12, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. ET Loeb Connect participation request deadline: November 30, 2026, for applicants planning to apply for the 2027–28 class The Fellowship advises applicants to begin working on their applications and recommendations well before the final deadline. Recommendation requests can be initiated before the applicant has completed the entire application. Who Should Apply for the Harvard Loeb Fellowship? The Fellowship is designed for mid-career professionals , rather than students or people who are just beginning their careers. Applicants are expected to have a minimum of eight years of professional experience in their field . The program is looking for practitioners who demonstrate: Exceptional professional skill Leadership ability A commitment to helping others succeed A strong record of professional work A desire to make a meaningful difference in their field The potential to develop their abilities further An interest in improving the built or natural environment The capacity to use the Fellowship experience to make a broader impact The program notes that a typical Loeb class averages approximately 42 years of age , but the stated eligibility requirement is based on professional experience and the applicant s stage of career rather than a specific age limit. You Do Not Need to Be an Architect or Designer One of the important features of the Harvard Loeb Fellowship is its broad definition of professional practice. Applicants do not necessarily have to identify as designers. The Fellowship has previously welcomed professionals working across different disciplines, including public artists, journalists, theatre directors, documentary filmmakers, architects, landscape architects, and urban planners. The central consideration is whether the applicant s work contributes to improving the built or natural environment and has broader social impact. Therefore, professionals with interdisciplinary or unconventional careers should not automatically assume that they are ineligible simply because their job title does not correspond to a traditional design profession. Is a University Degree Required? No. A completed higher-education degree is not a requirement for admission to the Loeb Fellowship. The Fellowship states that it values a creative and motivated work history and a commitment to supporting others over more traditional credentials. Professionals with unusual career paths or atypical backgrounds are encouraged to apply if they have demonstrated the ability to make a difference in their fields. Applicants who have obtained university degrees may include their educational information in their resumes, but applicants are not required to have a degree in order to apply. The program also states that it does not review academic transcripts . Are International Applicants Eligible? Yes. The Harvard Loeb Fellowship is not restricted to U.S. citizens . International candidates are specifically encouraged to apply. Successful international applicants will need to obtain a J-1 visa and must therefore be eligible to obtain the appropriate visa at the time of selection. This makes the Fellowship accessible to qualified practitioners from outside the United States, provided they satisfy the program s professional requirements and can meet the applicable visa requirements if selected. What Is the Loeb Fellowship Looking For? The Fellowship is designed for professionals who are at an important stage in their careers: experienced enough to have developed substantial expertise, but still positioned to use that experience to create further impact. The program describes the ideal candidates as people who have enough professional experience to ask difficult questions while still having considerable time remaining in their careers to apply what they learn. This means the Fellowship is not simply intended as recognition for past achievements. It is also intended to provide an opportunity for professional renewal, reflection, experimentation, and development. Applicants should therefore be prepared to demonstrate not only what they have accomplished, but also how they have developed as practitioners and how additional time, resources, networks, and intellectual engagement could contribute to their future work. The Fellowship Is for Practitioners, Not Students The Loeb Fellowship makes an important distinction between professional practice and academic study. It is not a student program and is not intended for people who are applying to Harvard Graduate School of Design as students. It is also generally not intended as a traditional academic sabbatical. Academics may potentially qualify in limited circumstances if more than 50 percent of their time is devoted to professional practice and they satisfy the other requirements. However, the program advises individuals in this situation to contact the Fellowship to discuss their eligibility. What Does the Harvard Loeb Fellowship Application Require? Applicants are required to submit an online application. The standard application includes: Completed online application Three letters of recommendation Professional resume Applicants can also submit supplemental materials, including a portfolio and other examples of their professional work. The application is completed online through SlideRoom, and applicants are required to register before submitting their materials. Applicants are advised to answer all questions on the application form while paying attention to the suggested response lengths. Three Letters of Recommendation Are Required Applicants must provide three professional recommendations . The program recommends choosing people who know the applicant and their professional work well. Potential recommenders may include: Colleagues Clients Collaborators Other individuals with substantive knowledge of the applicant s work The strongest recommendations are expected to come from people who can provide meaningful insight into the applicant s professional accomplishments, abilities, character as a practitioner, and contribution to their field. The recommendations are confidential and are not available to the applicant. When Are Recommendation Letters Due? Recommendation letters are due seven days after the main application deadline . For the 2027–28 Fellowship, the recommendation deadline is: Tuesday, January 12, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. ET. Applicants should not wait until the final application deadline to begin communicating with their recommenders. Once an applicant enters a recommender s name and contact information into SlideRoom, the system sends the recommender a request. The applicant does not need to finish the entire application before the recommendation request can be triggered. Applicants are also advised to remind recommenders to check their spam or junk folders because the request will come from SlideRoom rather than directly from the Loeb Fellowship. What Should Be Included in the Resume? Applicants must submit a professional resume that includes the dates of their work history . If an applicant has earned university degrees, the resume should include: Name of the educational institution Full name of the degree Year the degree was awarded Applicants should avoid relying solely on academic credentials because the Loeb Fellowship emphasizes professional accomplishments and practice. Portfolio and Supplemental Materials Applicants may also submit a portfolio or supplemental materials demonstrating their professional work. Examples of materials that may be submitted include: Articles Books Videos Visual representations Lectures Other materials that demonstrate the applicant s work These materials are optional , but the Fellowship strongly encourages applicants to submit up to five documents illustrating their work. Applicants should be strategic when selecting these materials. Because the Selection Committee has limited time to review applications, supplemental materials should communicate the applicant s work clearly and effectively rather than overwhelming reviewers with excessive information. Is There an Application Fee? No. There is no fee to apply for the Harvard Loeb Fellowship . How Does the Loeb Fellowship Selection Process Work? The selection process involves multiple stages. A Selection Committee reviews submitted applications. The committee consists of: Three faculty members from the Graduate School of Design Three Loeb Fellowship alumni Two outside practitioners The curator of the program The committee initially selects approximately 20 shortlisted applicants by the end of February . Applicants are expected to receive information about their application status by mid-March . Shortlisted candidates may then participate in up to three separate interviews: An interview with the Curator An interview with a member of the Selection Committee A third interview with someone familiar with the program The committee meets in mid-April to select up to 10 Fellows , with selected Fellows expected to be notified by the end of April. The Loeb/ArtLab Fellowship Applicants who are interested in the Loeb/ArtLab Fellowship can also indicate that interest during the application process. The Loeb Fellowship and Harvard ArtLab have established a joint fellowship designed to support artists whose practices and research align with the objectives of the Loeb Fellowship. The Loeb/ArtLab Fellowship is intended for innovative artists whose work focuses on improving the built and natural environment while encouraging: Interdisciplinary exchange Experimentation Public engagement Research Creative development Selected artists receive the Loeb Fellowship experience together with additional benefits connected to ArtLab, including studio space in the ArtLab building, research support, and networking opportunities through the ArtLab community. What Are Fellows Expected to Do During the Fellowship? The Loeb Fellowship requires Fellows to make a significant commitment to the program. Fellows must agree to step away from significant roles with their employers and from other substantial professional responsibilities during the Fellowship year. This includes activities such as major professional engagements, speaking commitments, and conferences. Fellows are also required to: Audit at least one GSD course per semester Remain in residence in the Cambridge area while classes are in session Participate in Fellowship programs Take part in weekly seminars Participate in weekly dinners with invited guests Join fall and spring study tours Participate in retreats and other activities organized by the Fellowship Engage with Harvard students and faculty Participate in the broader life of the Graduate School of Design Make use of resources available through Harvard University and MIT These requirements demonstrate that the Fellowship is intended to be an immersive professional and intellectual experience rather than simply a financial award or period away from work. Fellows Develop Individual Work Plans Each Fellow develops an individual work plan with input from program staff. The plan can be updated throughout the Fellowship year as the Fellow s priorities and work develop. At the conclusion of the Fellowship, a summary of the results of the work plan is included in the program s final report. This individualized approach allows Fellows to use their time according to their professional interests while remaining connected to the broader objectives and activities of the program. Can Fellows Bring Their Families? Yes. The Loeb Fellowship states that its resources can support families of modest size, and many Fellows bring their families to Cambridge during the Fellowship year. The program also notes that family members can benefit from the opportunities available in Harvard and Cambridge. Families with school-aged children should be aware that Cambridge Public Schools use a lottery system for school selection, and families should consult the relevant Cambridge Public Schools information for details. When Does the Fellowship Year Begin? Fellows generally arrive in mid-August , approximately one week before classes begin. There is an orientation period of approximately three to four days before classes start, and Fellows are advised to allow time to settle into the Cambridge area. The precise dates depend on the academic calendar for the relevant year. When Does the Fellowship Year End? The program officially ends on the day after commencement. Some Fellows, particularly those with children attending schools in the area, may remain in Cambridge through the end of the school year, which is generally around the second or third week of June. However, Fellows must leave their Fellowship housing by June 30 at the latest . What Happens After the Fellowship? Completion of the Loeb Fellowship does not mark the end of the relationship with the program. The Fellowship describes itself as a lifelong connection. Graduates join a worldwide network of more than 450 alumni . Fellows become alumni of both the Graduate School of Design and the Loeb Fellowship and can participate in the GSD alumni community and events while receiving applicable alumni benefits. This alumni network can provide an ongoing professional connection to other practitioners working across different disciplines and geographic regions. The Loeb Connect Alumni Program Potential applicants who are unfamiliar with the Loeb Fellowship, the GSD, or Harvard can participate in an optional opportunity to connect directly with Loeb alumni. The purpose of this initiative is to give prospective applicants an opportunity to have informal conversations about the Fellowship and learn more about the experience from people who have already participated. Participation is: Open to potential applicants Optional Not a requirement for applying Not considered as part of the admissions or selection process For individuals planning to apply for the 2027–28 class , participation should be requested by November 30, 2026 . Information Sessions for Prospective Applicants The Loeb Fellowship is also offering two Zoom webinars for prospective applicants. The sessions are scheduled for Monday, November 9 , with one session at 8:00 a.m. ET and another at 4:00 p.m. ET . The webinars are intended to help interested candidates learn more about the Fellowship and ask questions. The presentation will subsequently be recorded and made available on the Loeb Fellowship website together with answers to questions raised during the sessions. Reapplying to the Harvard Loeb Fellowship Individuals who applied in a previous year and want to apply again must submit a new application through the online system. A new application includes the required application information and supporting materials, including: Contact information Application forms Resume Portfolio, where applicable Supplemental materials, where applicable Recommendation letters from the immediate previous application year remain available to the program. However, applicants are advised to obtain at least one new recommendation that reflects work completed during the intervening period. Recommendation letters from earlier years will not be accepted. Important Considerations Before Applying Prospective applicants should carefully assess whether the Fellowship aligns with their professional circumstances before submitting an application. The program is particularly appropriate for practitioners who: Have at least eight years of professional experience Are established in their fields Have demonstrated leadership Have a record of meaningful professional work Work in areas connected to the built or natural environment Are interested in broader social impact Are prepared to step away from significant professional responsibilities for the Fellowship year Want to reflect on their professional experience and develop new capacities Are prepared to participate actively in the Harvard GSD community Applicants should also understand that the Fellowship is not simply an academic study opportunity. It requires active participation, residence in the Cambridge area during relevant periods, coursework, seminars, study tours, dinners, retreats, and engagement with the Harvard community. Harvard Loeb Fellowship 2027–28 Application Checklist Before submitting an application, prospective candidates should ensure that they have prepared the necessary materials and understand the key dates. Application materials Completed online application Professional resume Three professional recommendation letters Portfolio and/or supplemental materials, if desired Relevant work samples, with up to five supplemental documents strongly encouraged Before submission Applicants should: Review the Fellowship s eligibility requirements. Confirm that they have at least eight years of professional experience. Consider how their work relates to the built or natural environment and broader social impact. Prepare a clear professional resume. Identify three appropriate professional recommenders. Enter recommender information into SlideRoom early. Select strong supplemental materials that clearly demonstrate their work. Ensure digital materials are uploaded correctly. Submit the completed application before the deadline. Follow up with recommenders to ensure their letters are submitted by the separate recommendation deadline. Key Dates at a Glance Event Date Loeb Connect request deadline for 2027–28 applicants November 30, 2026 Prospective applicant webinars November 9, 2026 Main application deadline January 5, 2027, 11:59 p.m. ET Recommendation deadline January 12, 2027, 11:59 p.m. ET Approximately 20 applicants shortlisted By end of February Applicant status notifications Mid-March Final selection of up to 10 Fellows Mid-April Selected Fellows notified By end of April Fellowship begins Mid-August Latest housing departure June 30 The dates above are based on the information provided for the 2027–28 Fellowship cycle. How to Apply for the Harvard Loeb Fellowship Applicants should first carefully review the Fellowship s application information and frequently asked questions before beginning the application. The official application is submitted online through SlideRoom . Applicants must register on the platform and complete the required application questions. All supplemental materials must be submitted digitally because the Selection Committee does not review hard copies. Applicants experiencing technical problems with SlideRoom are advised to first consult SlideRoom Help and, if necessary, contact the Loeb Fellowship office regarding unresolved upload problems. CLICK HERE TO APPLY Frequently Asked Questions About the Harvard Loeb Fellowship Can someone who is not a designer apply? Yes. The Fellowship has a broad definition of professional practice and has welcomed practitioners from a variety of disciplines. Can current students apply? No. The Fellowship is intended for practitioners with at least eight years of professional experience. Do applicants need a university degree? No. A completed higher-education degree is not required. Do applicants have to be U.S. citizens? No. International applicants are encouraged to apply. Is there an application fee? No. Applying to the Loeb Fellowship is free. Are academic transcripts required? No. Academic transcripts are not reviewed. Are recommendation letters required? Yes. Three professional recommendation letters are required. When are recommendation letters due? For the 2027–28 Fellowship, recommendations are due January 12, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. ET , seven days after the main application deadline. Can applicants submit portfolios? Yes. Portfolios and supplemental materials are optional but strongly encouraged. Can Fellows bring their families? Yes. The Fellowship states that its resources can support families of modest size, and many Fellows bring their families. Do Fellows have to live in Cambridge? Fellows are required to remain in residence in the Cambridge area while classes are in session and participate in the Fellowship s activities. CLICK HERE for more information about the Harvard Loeb Fellowship 2027–28 Conclusion The Harvard Loeb Fellowship 2027–28 provides an opportunity for experienced practitioners to step away from their regular professional responsibilities and spend a year developing new ideas, expanding their skills, engaging with Harvard s academic and professional communities, and planning the next phase of their careers. The Fellowship is particularly notable for its broad approach to eligibility. Applicants do not have to follow a traditional academic or professional path, and a university degree is not required. What matters is substantial professional experience, demonstrated ability, leadership potential, a commitment to supporting others, and work connected to improving the built or natural environment and creating broader social impact. International professionals are encouraged to apply, and there is no application fee. Candidates should, however, carefully consider the Fellowship s substantial participation requirements, including residence in Cambridge, coursework, seminars, study tours, retreats, and engagement with the Harvard Graduate School of Design community. For professionals who meet the requirements and are considering applying, the most important date to remember is January 5, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. ET , when the main application closes. Recommendation letters have a separate deadline of January 12, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. ET . The source also provides an application route through SlideRoom for the 2027–28 Loeb Fellowship . title: DIViNE Doctoral Network 2026–2027: 10 PhD Positions in Political Violence, Democracy and Democratic Resilience Across Europe
summary: The DIViNE Doctoral Network (Democratic Institutions and Violence Network in Europe) is offering an exciting opportunity for aspiring researchers interested in democracy, political violence, conflict, institutional change, and democratic resilience. The network is designed to develop a new generation of interdisciplinary researchers capable of examining why political violence persists, changes, or is contained within democratic societies. It brings together leading European research institutions and international partner organizations, combining quantitative research, behavioral and experimental methods, historical and archival research, institutional theory, and policy engagement. As part of the initiative, DIViNE plans to hire 10 PhD researchers , with two researchers associated with each of the five principal university nodes. In addition, the Political Institutions and Conflict – Max Planck Institute in Göttingen will offer one further non-MSCA PhD scholarship. The current opportunity is an Expression of Interest (EOI) rather than the final PhD application. Interested candidates are invited to submit their expressions of interest by October 10, 2026 . The formal PhD vacancy calls are expected to be published between October and November 2026 , with PhD positions starting by January 2027 . What Is the DIViNE Doctoral Network? DIViNE stands for Democratic Institutions and Violence Network in Europe . The network addresses a central research puzzle: although democracies are generally associated with institutionalized political competition and nonviolent forms of contestation, democratic societies can still experience different forms of political violence. These forms of violence can include: Riots Electoral intimidation Extremist mobilization Organized political violence Criminal violence with political dimensions State and non-state violence Repression Militarized responses to perceived threats Political violence can challenge democratic institutions and norms. At the same time, governments responding to violence or perceived security threats may introduce measures that themselves create tensions with democratic principles. Examples include: Militarized policing Emergency legislation Selective repression Expanded security measures Restrictions on civil liberties Institutional responses that affect impartiality or the rule of law DIViNE seeks to examine these relationships systematically by bringing together researchers from different academic traditions and methodological backgrounds. The Central Research Problem A key concern of DIViNE is understanding how and why political violence persists, transforms, or becomes contained within democracies . This involves studying both the causes and consequences of violence. Researchers may investigate questions such as: Why does political violence continue after countries democratize? How do historical experiences of violence affect contemporary politics? How do democratic institutions respond to violent challenges? Why do some populations support or tolerate political violence? How do governments respond to violent movements? Can democratic reforms reduce political conflict? Under what circumstances can reforms unintentionally create new incentives for violence? How does militarization affect democratic institutions? How can democratic institutions and civil society strengthen resilience against political violence? The network approaches these questions from historical, institutional, behavioral, comparative, and methodological perspectives. DIViNE PhD Positions 2026–2027 DIViNE plans to recruit: 10 PhD researchers The researchers will be distributed across the five main university nodes, with: 2 PhD researchers at the University of Amsterdam 2 PhD researchers at the University of Essex 2 PhD researchers at the University of Milan 2 PhD researchers at Carlos III University of Madrid 2 PhD researchers at Uppsala University In addition, the Political Institutions and Conflict – Max Planck Institute in Göttingen will offer one further non-MSCA PhD scholarship . The positions are intended for researchers whose interests align with the broader research agenda of DIViNE. Important: This Is Currently an Expression of Interest Prospective applicants should understand that the current announcement is not yet the final PhD vacancy application . DIViNE is currently inviting candidates to submit an Expression of Interest . The formal PhD vacancy calls are expected to be published: Between October and November 2026 Formal applications will subsequently need to be submitted through the relevant DIViNE university webpages. Therefore, submitting an expression of interest is an important preliminary step, but candidates should also monitor the relevant university websites for the official PhD vacancy announcements. Expression of Interest Deadline The deadline to submit the current expression of interest is: October 10, 2026 Interested candidates should submit their expression of interest through the form provided by DIViNE. Submit the DIViNE Expression of Interest What Information Is Required for the Expression of Interest? The expression of interest asks candidates to provide information in four main areas. 1. Bachelor s and Master s Information Applicants will need to provide information about their: Bachelor s degree Master s degree Academic background Candidates should therefore have their relevant academic information available when completing the form. 2. Motivation and Research Idea Applicants will be asked to explain: Why they are interested in the program Their proposed research idea Their research question Relevant literature Their theoretical or substantive argument Their proposed methods This section is particularly important because it gives applicants an opportunity to demonstrate how their academic interests connect with the DIViNE research agenda. A good research idea should be sufficiently focused to communicate a clear research question while demonstrating awareness of relevant academic debates. 3. Selected Work Package or Research Theme Applicants will need to identify the Work Package(s) (WP) that interest them. They will also be asked to provide a short explanation of: Why they are interested in the selected theme Why their research background fits the theme How their proposed research connects with the selected research area Applicants should therefore carefully examine the DIViNE research themes before selecting their preferred area. 4. Two Referees Candidates must provide the names of two referees who will support their application. Applicants should consider selecting referees who are familiar with their academic background and can provide relevant information about their research abilities and potential. DIViNE s Two Main Objectives The Doctoral Training Network has two overarching ambitions. Objective 1: Advance Scientific Understanding The network aims to improve scientific understanding of: Why political violence persists How political violence changes Why violence becomes contained in some democratic settings How institutions respond to violent challenges How historical experiences influence contemporary politics Objective 2: Train a New Generation of Interdisciplinary Scholars DIViNE also aims to train researchers who can conduct: Cross-disciplinary research Multi-method research Scientifically rigorous research Policy-relevant research Research relevant to stakeholders and institutions This means the program is not focused solely on developing theoretical academic knowledge. It also emphasizes the ability to produce research that can engage with real-world policy and institutional questions. The Four DIViNE Research Themes The network organizes its research around four major themes. 1. Conflict Inheritance and Legacies in Democracies This theme investigates how historical violence continues to influence contemporary democratic politics. Researchers examine issues such as: Historical violence Repression Institutional legacies Transitional compromises Contemporary political behavior Institutional functioning A central question is how experiences from the past can continue to shape political institutions and behavior long after the original conflict has ended. 2. Democratization and Conflict Resolution The second theme focuses on political reforms introduced during democratic transitions and their consequences for violence and reconciliation. Potential areas of research include: Transitional justice Decentralization Land reform Territorial reform Constitutional redesign Power-sharing Political reconciliation The research examines whether such reforms reduce conflict, create incentives for cooperation, or sometimes generate unintended consequences. 3. Dynamics of Support for Violent Movements and Responses The third research theme focuses on the individual and societal foundations of support for political violence. It examines questions such as: Why do people support political violence? Why do some people tolerate violence? How do violent organizations cultivate legitimacy? How do state actors develop legitimacy for coercive responses? What causes people to support or reject violent movements? This theme places particular emphasis on the micro-foundations of political violence. 4. Democratic Resilience and Violent Stress The fourth theme examines how democratic institutions respond when they face violent or security-related pressures. Research can focus on: Institutional design Public policy Civil society Securitization Militarization Democratic resilience Institutional responses to violence A key concern is whether responses to violence strengthen democratic resilience or unintentionally create conditions that contribute to democratic erosion. Ten Doctoral Candidate Research Themes The network identifies ten specific research themes for doctoral candidates. DC1 — Historical Legacies of Violence and Democratic Institutions This research area examines the relationship between historical experiences of violence and the functioning of democratic institutions. DC2 — Exogenous Shocks, Violent Legacies, and Democratic Resilience This theme examines how external shocks and existing legacies of violence interact with democratic resilience. DC3 — Endogenous Persistence of Violence After Democratization This research area focuses on why violence can persist within countries even after democratization. DC4 — The Unintended Consequences of Democratic Reforms This theme investigates situations in which reforms intended to strengthen democracy or resolve conflict produce unexpected consequences. DC5 — Institutional Reform, Violence, and Democratic Consolidation This research examines the relationship between institutional reform, political violence, and the consolidation of democratic systems. DC6 — Security Externalities and Post-Conflict Democratization This theme explores security consequences associated with post-conflict democratization. DC7 — Public Support for Political Violence in Advanced Democracies This research area focuses on public attitudes toward political violence within established democratic settings. DC8 — Militarization, Public Support, and Democratic Erosion in Latin America This theme examines relationships among militarization, public attitudes, and democratic erosion in Latin American contexts. DC9 — Democratic Decline, Political Violence, and Cycles of Repression This research area examines interactions between democratic decline, political violence, and repression. DC10 — Recruitment Dynamics and Behavioral Output of Violent Organizations This theme focuses on how violent organizations recruit participants and how recruitment relates to organizational behavior. Universities and Research Institutions in the DIViNE Network DIViNE brings together five principal European university research environments: University of Amsterdam (UvA) University of Essex (UESSEX) University of Milan (UMIL) Carlos III University of Madrid (UC3M) Uppsala University (UU) Together, these institutions contribute complementary research expertise to the network. The research environment combines several methodological and disciplinary approaches. These include: Quantitative conflict research Behavioral research Experimental methods Historical research Archival research Institutional theory Normative theory Policy engagement This interdisciplinary structure is one of the defining characteristics of the doctoral network. Faculty and PhD Supervisors The network includes a group of researchers who will supervise doctoral candidates across the participating institutions. The listed faculty members are: Giulia Bistagnino — University of Milan Simon Chauchard — Carlos III University of Madrid Ursula Daxecker — University of Amsterdam / MPI Annekatrin Deglow — Uppsala University Hanne Fjelde — Uppsala University Ismene Gizelis — University of Essex Kristian S. Gleditsch — University of Essex Kathleen Klaus — Uppsala University Juan Masullo — University of Milan Brian Phillips — University of Essex Paola Rebughini — University of Milan Andrea Ruggeri — University of Milan Ignacio Sánchez-Cuenca — Carlos III University of Madrid Jessica Soedirgo — University of Amsterdam Abbey Steele — University of Amsterdam Francisco Villamil — Carlos III University of Madrid The range of faculty expertise reflects the network s interdisciplinary approach to studying political violence and democratic institutions. Research Partners and PhD Research Stays DIViNE PhD researchers will also have research stays with partner organizations associated with the network. Partners include: Action on Armed Violence (AOAV) Barcelona Centre for International Affairs (CIDOB) Clingendael — Netherlands Institute of International Relations Fondazione Giangiacomo Feltrinelli International Catalan Institute for Peace (ICIP) International IDEA Political Institutions and Conflict – Max Planck Institute in Göttingen These partnerships can expose doctoral researchers to research environments beyond universities and provide opportunities to engage with organizations working on conflict, peace, governance, and international affairs. International and Interdisciplinary Research Environment One of the central features of DIViNE is its combination of different research methods. Political violence is a complex phenomenon, and the network approaches it from multiple perspectives. Quantitative Conflict Research Quantitative methods can be used to examine patterns of conflict and political violence across countries, regions, and time periods. Behavioral and Experimental Methods Behavioral and experimental research can help investigate how individuals perceive political violence, institutions, security, and political movements. Historical and Archival Research Historical and archival approaches allow researchers to examine how past political violence, repression, and institutional arrangements influence contemporary political behavior. Institutional and Normative Theory The network also incorporates theoretical approaches to understanding democratic institutions, political authority, legitimacy, and institutional responses to violence. Policy Engagement The program aims to produce research that is not only scientifically rigorous but also relevant to policymakers and other stakeholders. Mobility Requirements for PhD Researchers An important requirement applies to researchers recruited through the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) framework. PhD researchers recruited to the project must satisfy the relevant MSCA mobility requirements . In particular, they must not have: Resided or worked for more than one year in the country of the institution where they are enrolled. Applicants should therefore carefully assess their residence and employment history before applying. The doctoral program will also involve mobility across institutions and partners within the network . This means that doctoral researchers should be prepared for an international and mobile research experience rather than remaining exclusively at a single institution throughout the program. When Will the PhD Positions Start? The DIViNE announcement states that PhD positions are expected to start by January 2027 . The formal vacancy calls are expected to be published between: October and November 2026 Candidates interested in the positions should therefore monitor the relevant DIViNE university webpages after submitting their expression of interest. Step 1: Review Your Academic Background Prepare information about your: Bachelor s degree Master s degree Research experience Academic interests Relevant coursework Previous research projects Step 2: Identify Your Research Area Review the four major research themes and ten doctoral research themes. Consider which area most closely matches your interests. Step 3: Develop a Research Idea Prepare a preliminary research idea that includes: A clear research question Relevant literature A potential argument Possible research methods A clear connection to political violence and democratic institutions Step 4: Consider Your Preferred Work Package Identify the Work Package or research theme that interests you most and think about why your background makes you a good fit. Step 5: Identify Two Referees Choose two academic referees who can support your application. Contact them in advance so they are aware of your interest in the program. The formal PhD vacancies are expected to be published between October and November 2026. Why Consider the DIViNE Doctoral Network? DIViNE offers an opportunity to develop doctoral research within a large European research network focused on important questions surrounding democracy and political violence. title: Google Scholarships 2026: 7 Scholarship Opportunities for Students in Computer Science and Technology

Some are designed for students in the United States and Canada, while others focus on Europe or India. The programme encourages students who combine an interest in computer science with a desire to create positive environmental and social change. Focus of the Venkat Panchapakesan Memorial Scholarship The scholarship looks for students who demonstrate qualities such as: Passion for computer science Optimism Commitment to education Interest in sustainability Desire to use technology to address global challenges The opportunity can be particularly relevant to students who want to combine technology with sustainability and use their future careers to contribute to solutions for environmental and societal challenges. Research the Specific Scholarship The most important step is to review the requirements of the specific scholarship you intend to apply for. Conclusion Google offers a diverse collection of scholarship and grant opportunities designed to support students and individuals pursuing education and professional development in computer science, technology, and related fields . title: 100x Impact £150,000 Funding Opportunity for High-Impact Ventures: Eligibility, Benefits and Application Process
summary: The 100x Impact funding opportunity is seeking ambitious organisations with the potential to improve the lives of hundreds of millions or even billions of people. Through the programme, selected ventures can receive £150,000 in catalytic funding , together with a long-term partnership designed to help organisations strengthen their strategies, measure their impact, develop leadership capacity, and build pathways to scale. The programme is aimed at organisations that are already working on important social or environmental challenges and have demonstrated solutions that could potentially achieve significant scale. In addition to financial support, selected ventures can gain access to strategic support, research expertise from the London School of Economics (LSE) , and connections to a global network of funders, advisers, partners, and peer organisations. About the 100x Impact Opportunity 100x is looking to partner with what it describes as future social unicorns : organisations capable of creating positive change at a very large scale. The programme looks beyond organisations that simply have an interesting idea. Applicants are expected to demonstrate that they have a proven solution, a clear understanding of the problem they are addressing, evidence of performance, a capable team, and a realistic pathway to scale. The programme also places emphasis on organisations that are close to the communities they serve and have the potential to contribute to broader systemic transformation. What Selected Ventures Will Receive Selected organisations will receive a combination of financial support, strategic assistance, research expertise, and access to networks. £150,000 in Catalytic Funding Selected ventures will receive £150,000 in catalytic funding . The funding is intended to strengthen the organisation s pathway to scale. Rather than being presented simply as financial support, the funding is connected to the broader objective of helping ventures increase their impact and reach. Long-Term Partnership Selected ventures will enter into a long-term partnership with 100x. The partnership begins with a tailored 16-week programme designed to help organisations strengthen important areas of their work. Support can include: Developing a stronger funding strategy Improving impact measurement Strengthening leadership Preparing the organisation for growth Identifying pathways to scale Developing strategies for long-term impact Access to Advisers, Funders and Partners Selected ventures will also gain connections to advisers, funders, partners, and other organisations within the 100x community. These connections can provide opportunities for organisations to: Exchange ideas Build professional relationships Learn from peers Explore potential partnerships Identify funding opportunities Access relevant expertise Potential Follow-On Funding Some selected ventures may also have the potential to receive additional funding in the future. However, follow-on funding is not guaranteed and will depend on factors including the fit between the venture and available funding. 100x Impact Eligibility Criteria 100x outlines several key eligibility areas that applicants should consider before applying. 1. Impact-First Venture Applicants should be organisations that put social or environmental impact at the centre of their work. The organisation should be focused on solving a significant problem rather than simply pursuing commercial growth without a clear impact objective. 2. Focus on an Impact Area The organisation must be focused on one of 100x s eight Impact Areas . Applicants should therefore ensure that their work clearly aligns with one of the areas identified by 100x before submitting an application. 3. Proven Solution 100x is looking for organisations with solutions that have already demonstrated evidence of working. Applicants should be prepared to demonstrate how their solution addresses the problem they are tackling and provide evidence of its effectiveness. The programme is focused on organisations with existing models and approaches rather than ventures that are only at the idea stage. 4. Ambition for Scale A central feature of this opportunity is the ambition to reach very large numbers of people. 100x is searching for organisations with the potential to improve the lives of hundreds of millions or even billions of people . Applicants should therefore be able to explain how their organisation could expand its reach and impact over time. 5. End-User Reach The programme considers the number of people who benefit from an organisation s solution. Applicants should be able to demonstrate their existing reach and explain how they intend to expand that reach. 6. Team Size The organisation s team is also considered as part of the application and selection process. 100x takes a holistic approach that considers not only the solution itself but also the people leading and delivering it. Selection Criteria 100x evaluates applications using several broad criteria. Problem Applicants should clearly demonstrate their understanding of the problem they are trying to solve. The problem should be significant enough to justify the scale of ambition expected by the programme. Proposition The organisation should have a clear proposition that explains how its solution addresses the identified problem. Applicants should be able to demonstrate why their approach is relevant and how it creates positive change. Performance Evidence of performance is important. Organisations should be able to demonstrate what they have achieved so far and provide evidence supporting the effectiveness of their model. People 100x considers the people behind the organisation. This includes the leadership team and the broader capabilities required to execute the organisation s strategy and pursue growth. Pathways Applicants should demonstrate a credible pathway for expanding their impact. This means explaining how the organisation can move from its current level of reach to substantially greater levels of impact. 100x Additionality The programme also considers whether 100x s involvement could make a meaningful difference to the organisation. Applicants should consider what additional value the funding, strategic support, research expertise, networks, and partnership could provide to their organisation. Focus on Emerging Markets 100x states that it aims to have 70% of its portfolio come from emerging markets . The organisation also values applications where founders or senior team members are based in the region in which the organisation operates. This reflects an emphasis on proximity to communities and local leadership. Organisations operating in emerging markets can therefore highlight their connection to the communities they serve and explain how their leadership and operating model are connected to those communities. What the Application Process Looks Like The application process consists of several stages. Stage 1: Online Application and Review The application window remains open for five weeks . 100x encourages ventures to apply as early as possible during the application period. After applications are submitted, the 100x team reviews them carefully. Based on this initial assessment, up to 50 teams will be selected to progress to the next stage. Teams that do not progress will be notified in December 2026 . Stage 2: Initial Interview Selected organisations will proceed to an initial interview. The interview is generally conducted online and is expected to last approximately 20 minutes . The conversation may involve founders or senior leaders of the organisation. The purpose is to help 100x understand: The people leading the organisation The organisation s solution The problem being addressed The organisation s plans for the future The potential pathway to scale Interviews will be arranged through email. Stage 3: Detailed Due Diligence Organisations that progress beyond the initial interview will enter a more detailed due diligence process. At this stage, the time and resources required from the applicant increase significantly. 100x will request additional information and conduct more detailed conversations with the team. The due diligence process generally involves approximately two to three hours of online conversations , together with follow-up requests for specific information. For the current application cycle, this stage is scheduled to take place between January and April 2027 . Applicants should therefore be prepared to commit significant time and resources if they reach this stage. Stage 4: Cohort Selection Following due diligence, applications are reviewed by an independent selection committee . The committee makes the final selection decisions for the cohort. The outcome of the selection process is expected to be communicated in July 2027 . Stage 5: Programme Start Organisations that are selected will then be connected with the 100x Programme team. The Programme team will support successful ventures through the onboarding process and provide additional information about: Programme schedules Kick-off week Programme activities Expectations for participating organisations Who Is This Opportunity Designed For? The opportunity is designed for ambitious organisations that have already developed and demonstrated a solution to a significant social or environmental problem. It may be particularly relevant to ventures that: Have a strong impact-first mission Have a proven solution Already reach a meaningful number of end users Have ambitious plans for growth Can demonstrate evidence of performance Have capable founders or senior leadership Have the potential to reach very large populations Can demonstrate a credible pathway to scale The programme is therefore not primarily designed for individuals applying independently. It is focused on organisations or ventures with an established model and a team capable of delivering that model. Applicants are encouraged to apply as soon as possible during the five-week application period rather than waiting until the end of the window. The organisation states that applicants who do not progress beyond the initial review will be notified in December 2026 . Important Dates in the Selection Process For organisations considering the opportunity, the main timeline provided is: Application period: Five weeks Initial application review: Following submission Notification for applicants who do not progress: December 2026 Detailed due diligence: January to April 2027 Final cohort selection outcome: July 2027 Programme: Begins after selected ventures are onboarded Visit HERE to learn more about the 100x Impact £150,000 Funding Opportunity for High-Impact Ventures How to Apply Interested organisations can apply through the official 100x application platform. Before applying, ventures should ensure that they can clearly communicate: The problem they are addressing Their proposed solution Evidence that the solution works Their current performance The people behind the organisation Their existing end-user reach Their ambitions for scale Their pathway to significantly greater impact Why 100x s support could provide additional value Applicants should also be prepared for a potentially intensive process if they progress beyond the initial application. Why the Opportunity Is Significant for High-Impact Ventures The 100x programme combines funding with long-term strategic support. For organisations seeking to scale, the opportunity provides access to resources beyond the initial £150,000 catalytic funding . The 16-week programme can help participating ventures strengthen their funding and impact measurement strategies, while leadership support can help organisations prepare for the challenges associated with growth. The network of advisers, funders, partners, and peers can also provide opportunities for knowledge sharing and relationship building. Conclusion The 100x Impact £150,000 funding opportunity is designed to identify and support ambitious organisations with the potential to achieve transformative impact at a very large scale. Selected ventures can receive £150,000 in catalytic funding , a long-term partnership, a tailored 16-week programme, strategic support, access to LSE s research expertise, and connections to funders, advisers, partners, and peers. The programme looks for organisations with a proven solution, strong performance, capable leadership, significant end-user reach, and a credible ambition and pathway for scale . 100x also states that it aims for 70% of its portfolio to come from emerging markets and values applications where founders or senior team members are based in the region where the organisation operates. The application window is open for five weeks , with applicants encouraged to apply early. Organisations that progress through the process may undergo interviews and detailed due diligence between January and April 2027, with final cohort outcomes expected in July 2027. For organisations that have developed proven solutions to major social or environmental problems and are seeking support to significantly expand their impact, this programme provides a combination of funding, strategic assistance, networks, and long-term partnership.
